title: Multi-region routing & failover: Runtime performance, KV cache, batching
summary: Deep dive on Redwood's multi-region routing and failover design focusing on policy routing, regional capacity, DR playbooks, and implications for runtime performance (latency/throughput), KV cache semantics, batching, and quantization. Discussed session affinity, cache warming, circuit breakers, SLOs, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Agreed next steps: share runbook, run a cross-region benchmark, and prepare a private deployment checklist.
topics: cache coherence and KV cache warming
quantization variants and compatibility across regions
next_steps: Redwood to share multi-region runbook and topology diagram (Marco)
Run cross-region latency/throughput benchmark targeting EU->US traffic (Priya + BlueOrbit)
Schedule follow-up to review benchmark results in 2 weeks
action_items: Marco Ruiz: export staged topology diagram + routing policy template by 2025-03-20
Priya Nair: coordinate cross-region load test and provide initial metrics by 2025-03-28
Ava Chen: share private deployment security checklist and KMS options by 2025-03-18
Liam O'Connor: provide list of priority regions and RTO/RPO targets by 2025-03-17
transcript:
[00:00] Ava: alright everyone welcome thanks for joining, this is the Redwood deep dive on multi-region routing and failover. we have about an hour. quick intros?
[00:07] Liam: hey I'm Liam, head of platform at BlueOrbit, thanks for doing this. we're trying to understand failure modes and perf impact if we route traffic across EU/US/APAC.
[00:14] Amy: Amy here, SRE, mostly focused on latency targets and cache correctness.
[00:18] Marco: Marco from Redwood SE team, I'll run through the routing options and the runtime implications.
[00:22] Carlos: Carlos, security. I want to confirm data residency and KMS constraints.
[00:26] Priya: Priya, Redwood SRE, i'll own the benchmark plan.
[00:30] Ava: great. quick agenda: routing policies, capacity failover, KV cache semantics, batching and tail latency, quantization compatibility, and DR playbook.
[00:38] Liam: perfect. one thing up front: we have strict EU data residency for EU customers, but we can route non-PII to US. how do you normally handle policy routing?
[00:46] Marco: good question. we support policy-based routing: you can set rules by region, customer tag, or endpoint. policies are evaluated in order; first-match wins. typical pattern: geo-preferred, then capacity fallback, then cost fallback. we also support a hard pin for compliance — that forces routing to a given region.
[01:05] Amy: when you say capacity fallback, is that per-model or per-tenant?
[01:09] Marco: per-deployment — typically per model version + routing table. we track regional pools; fallback is to a compatible model variant in another region (same quantization profile ideally).
[01:18] Liam: compatible variant... does that mean quantized models have to match across regions? we use quantized 4-bit for cost.
[01:23] Marco: yes, for deterministic latency characteristics you should keep quantization profiles consistent. mismatched quantization can change runtime kernels and memory layout; in a worst-case it may not be compatible, so Redwood's policy will only fallback to variants marked as compatible. we recommend a 'compatible family' tag on model versions.
[01:36] Nora: what about KV cache — if a session is pinned to region A and then fails over to region B, do you lose the KV cache? what is the strategy?
[01:42] Priya: short answer: unless you use global KV replication, yes you'll lose local KV cache. we have two options: global KV replication or cache rebuild/warmup. global replication reduces latency on failover but adds cross-region egress and higher write latencies.
[01:56] Amy: global replication sounds expensive for heavy write workloads. can you do sticky sessions to avoid cross-region hits?
[02:02] Marco: session affinity (sticky routing) is supported for N minutes, TTL configurable per route. affinity helps preserve KV cache locality. but if an entire region fails, affinity is healed and requests get routed to fallback region — which triggers a cold-KV path. that's why we recommend a hybrid approach: affinity + cache pre-warm for critical routes.
[02:18] Liam: cache pre-warm — can you explain typical patterns?
[02:21] Marco: sure. two main patterns: 1) proactive pre-warm where we replay recent prefixes or a selected prompt set to the fallback region and populate KV; 2) on-demand warm where the first requests pay the cold penalty but we accelerate warm-up by prioritizing caching for hot prefixes and using a prioritized batching queue. both have tradeoffs.
[02:38] Carlos: replaying payloads is a security concern for us — we need to ensure PII isn't replicated. how do you avoid that?
[02:44] Ava: we treat cache replication as opt-in at tenant level; customers can mark certain inputs as non-replicable, or we can use deterministic hashing to strip PII before replication. we also integrate with customer KMS so encrypted blobs don't expose plaintext in another region.
[02:58] Amy: ok that helps. moving to batching — if you route across regions, how does batching behave? does cross-region batching happen?
03:04 Marco: good spot, so batching is per-region runtime queue. we don't batch across regions because of RTT. however when traffic fails over we may see momentary batching profile changes that affect tail latency — for instance, region B's batch size and latency SLOs may differ. we have dynamic batch sizing by regional queue shape, and we surface batch metrics in console.
[03:25] Liam: can you quantify the tail latency impact if we switch regions? like 95th/99th percentiles?
[03:29] Priya: depends on config. rough rule: if the fallback region has similar hardware and quantization, p95 delta is usually +10-25ms, p99 can be +50-200ms during warm-up or cold-KV scenarios. big deltas occur when model variants differ or there is heavy batching in the fallback region.
[03:46] Amy: what about circuit breakers? we need automated backoff when region congestion spikes.
[03:50] Marco: we provide circuit-breakers at routing layer — based on queue-depth, RT, and error rates. policies can mark a region/unhealthy pool as degraded and route around it. there's also gradual failover (traffic shifting) and instant failover options.
[04:03] Carlos: any integration with our infra alerts? PagerDuty and Prometheus?
[04:06] Priya: yes we expose Prometheus metrics and webhooks; alerts can auto-trigger routing policy changes if you wire them into the Redwood control plane. we can add a small webhook playbook to flip a routing tag.
[04:16] Liam: let's talk SLOs and RTO/RPO. our compliance folks expect RTO < 5 minutes for inference availability. is that realistic?
[04:23] Marco: depends on plan and reserved capacity. with Dedicated pools and cross-region replication it's feasible. RTO is dominated by DNS/route propagation and cache warm-up. with pre-warmed standby and health-probes you can get sub-2 minute failover. without pre-warm you're looking at several minutes to tens of minutes depending on model size.
[04:40] Nora: DNS — do you rely on DNS TTLs? what's the typical mechanism for global traffic steering?
[04:44] Marco: we support multiple layers: edge routing via anycast + CDN, implicit routing via intelligent load balancer (regional proxy + route tables), and DNS-based failover for customer-managed endpoints. anycast helps keep routes but can be slow to withdraw. route table + health checks is our common approach for controlled shift.
[04:59] Ava: note: for Private deployments in customer VPC, we avoid public anycast; we rely on customer networking + BGP/route policies or SD-WAN. so that changes the playbook.
[05:09] Carlos: KMS question: if you replicate caches or artifacts cross-region, how do you handle KMS keys?
[05:13] Marco: we support customer-managed keys per region. for private deployments you'd bring your own KMS/HSM per region; for hosted we can integrate with cloud KMS and optionally wrap cross-region keys. key rotation and audit logs are surfaced.
[05:23] Amy: ok. can we step through a concrete DR scenario? say EU region loses power — what's the step-by-step?
[05:28] Priya: sure. high-level DR playbook: 1) health detection triggers region degraded tag (automatic probes) 2) routing policy marks region as fallback; gradual traffic shift begins per policy (can be immediate) 3) monitor cold-KV rates and prioritize cache warm tasks 4) adjust batch sizing and concurrency limits to avoid overwhelming fallback region 5) if security requires, run privacy filter on pre-warm data 6) post-mortem and rollback when original region healthy.
[05:52] Liam: that is helpful. what about read replicas for KV? you mentioned global replication earlier — what's the recommended consistency model?
[05:58] Marco: for KV cache we recommend eventual consistency with write-through for critical keys. Strong consistency is expensive cross-region. patterns: use local write-through + async replication for session metadata that can be reconstructed if lost. For transactional data, don't use KV cache; use your DB with proper replication.
[06:15] Amy: any tooling to estimate egress costs when enabling global KV replication?
[06:19] Marco: yes we have an optimizer that simulates cross-region egress given expected write volumes. we'll include that in the runbook we'll share.
[06:26] Nora: one more thing — how do you handle model rollouts across regions? we want canary in one region then roll to others.
[06:30] Marco: rollouts are per-region by default. you can do canary in region A, then promote model to region B. we keep model version pins per-route; you can set progressive rollout rules with auto-rollback on quality regressions. we also do staggered quantization conversion jobs to avoid incompatibility.
[06:48] Liam: what about the case when region B doesn't have the same GPU types — will fallback choose a slower hardware?
[06:52] Marco: yes, runtime selects kernels by hardware. fallback policy can specify hardware constraints; if fallback hardware is slower, you can apply a 'degraded mode' routing that reduces max tokens, forces low-cost quantization family, or enables stricter caching to protect latency. it's all policy-driven.
[07:10] Amy: that could be a lot of engineering on our side to define degraded modes. do you provide templates?
[07:14] Marco: yes, we provide degraded-mode templates: token caps, concurrency throttles, and fallback model mappings. we'll share the template.
[07:20] Ava: quick pause — any questions on observability?
[07:23] Liam: yes, we need per-token cost breakdown and per-route latency at 1s granularity for SLO auditing.
[07:29] Priya: console exposes token-level cost and per-route histograms; for very fine-grained we stream traces to your tracing backend. there's a small retention and sampling tradeoff.
[07:38] Carlos: audit logs for cross-region access — we need to show where data was processed.
[07:41] Marco: audit logs include region, node-id, and model-version. for private deployments we can increase retention and ship to your SIEM.
[07:49] Nora: can you show an example policy for geo-preferred with capacity fallback?
[07:53] Marco: example: 1) rule: if customer.region == EU then prefer EU pool; 2) rule: if EU pool healthy AND queue depth < threshold send to EU; 3) else if EU pool degraded route to EU-standby in nearby AZ; 4) else route to US-west fallback with tag 'compatible-quant-4bit' — with sticky-session TTL 15m. i'll paste the exact template after.
[08:12] Amy: paste please — also include health-check thresholds.
[08:15] Marco: will do. next, tail-latency mitigation: we talked about dynamic batching. we also expose a 'latency-sensitive' mode which reduces maximum batch size and raises CPU/GPU priority at the cost of throughput. it's useful for interactive flows.
[08:31] Liam: what about token-level caching (prefix cache) vs KV cache? do both replicate?
[08:36] Marco: prefix caching is local; we don't replicate full prefix caches cross-region. KV cache (session-derived key-value store) can be replicated. prefix caches are warmable by replaying common prefixes. best practice: replicate only metadata and hashed minimal context, avoid raw prefixes if PII concerns.
[08:50] Carlos: encryption in transit and at rest across regions?
[08:53] Marco: TLS in transit, and at-rest encryption using customer keys where required. for cross-region replication we can use envelope encryption and region-bound DEKs.
[08:59] Amy: we have a question from the engineering chat — how fast can you flip traffic? is this minutes or seconds?
[09:03] Priya: automatic mark-down can be seconds for internal route table flips, but DNS propagation is minutes. with our control plane + edge proxies you can get near-instant rerouting for traffic that hits our edge. for private VPC deployments flips depend on your network.
[09:18] Marco: important nuance: instant flips can cause a storm of cache-miss traffic to fallback region; we throttle and ramp traffic to avoid overload. that's where prioritized warm-up plays a role.
[09:28] Liam: about prioritized warm-up, can we define which prefixes are high priority?
[09:31] Marco: yes, we accept a priority list; you can attach weight to prefixes or session tags. we also have an ML-based hot-prefix predictor but it's opt-in.
[09:40] Amy: one of our core flows uses tool-calling and function outputs. are those preserved across failover? if a function call stores ephemeral state in a region, what happens?
[09:49] Marco: ephemeral tool states follow the same model: either replicate tool outputs (if allowed), or treat them as local. we recommend stateless tool implementations or using a global store with replication for tools that need state.
[09:59] Carlos: any compliance red flags we should be aware of? cross-region replication, keys, and audit visibility were mentioned.
[10:03] Marco: main compliance concerns: PII replication, KMS key residency, audit retention. we can configure per-tenant controls to block replication and require region-only processing. also possible to use on-prem/Private deployment for air-gapped needs.
[10:16] Liam: Private deployments — can two regions be connected via a private backbone so KV replication doesn't traverse public internet?
[10:22] Marco: yes: for Private we recommend direct connect / private interconnect between regions or customer SD-WAN. that keeps replication on private links and satisfies many compliance controls. Redwood can assist with network architecture.
[10:33] Nora: do you have any recommended RTO/RPO SLAs for different configs?
[10:37] Priya: template: Hosted w/o pre-warm: RTO 5-30m, RPO near-0 for durable stores but KV loses; Hosted + pre-warm + standby: RTO <2m, RPO near-0 for control plane, eventual for KV; Dedicated reserved capacity + replication: RTO <1m possible. On-prem depends on network but with pre-warm you can be sub-5m.
[10:58] Ava: moving on — instrumentation for post-failover analysis? what data do you keep?
[11:02] Marco: we keep request traces, model-version mapping, routing decisions, and cache-miss rates. timestamps and region tags are in the logs. we keep defaults at 90 days but can extend for enterprise.
[11:13] Amy: good. can you walk us through a sample routing table entry?
[11:17] Marco: sample: name: eu-payments-route; match: customer.tag==payments && geo==EU; actions: prefer pool eu-prod-primary; fallback: eu-prod-standby (weight 50%), us-west-fallback (weight 100, tag: compatible-quant-4bit); sticky_ttl: 900s; circuit_breaker: queue_depth>200 => mark degraded. i'll send the YAML.
[11:39] Liam: great. on the benchmarking side, what inputs should we run? e2e: cold KV, warm KV, pre-warm scenario?
[11:45] Priya: yes: 1) cold-start: simulate no KV and measure p50/p95/p99 across models; 2) warm: pre-populate KV and retest; 3) failover storm: flip 60% traffic to fallback and measure drop; 4) long-tail: sustained high QPS with steady-state. we'll provide test harness scripts.
[12:03] Nora: about test harness — do you support replaying production traces?
[12:06] Marco: yes, but we sanitize. we replay hashed prompts or anonymized traces. we can also run synthetic workloads with similar token-length distributions.
[12:15] Amy: quantization: you mentioned compatibility tags earlier. if we quantize differently in region B, will you block fallback?
[12:20] Marco: by default fallback is only to variants marked compatible. admins can override but it's risky because kernel differences can cause unexpected errors or poor perf.
[12:29] Liam: anything else about throughput throttles?
[12:32] Marco: yes, route-level QPS caps and token caps per second. we also support elastic backpressure signals to clients via headers for graceful degradation.
[12:43] Ava: security quick note: we'll share our SOC2 attachments and region-specific compliance docs. Carlos, anything specific you want added?
[12:49] Carlos: include explicit KMS per-region diagrams and the audit log retention policy. and a statement on whether pre-warmed caches ever persist plaintext outside EU.
[12:58] Ava: noted.
[13:00] Liam: let's role-play a specific DR exercise — you flip EU to degraded, how long until the first request in US sees a response?
[13:06] Priya: depends: if we have standby warmed it's milliseconds extra for network + processing; if not warmed, first request pays model load and KV misses — can be seconds to tens of seconds for large models. for our medium model family (7B-ish quantized) cold-model load is usually 1-3s, plus token generation.
[13:24] Marco: but note if the fallback region is heavily batched you'll see added queuing latency; that's why we throttle shifts.
[13:31] Amy: are there recommended thresholds for when to do instant vs phased failover?
[13:35] Marco: instant for clear hard failures (network partition); phased for degraded performance or rising error rates so you can measure and adjust. thresholds: error rate > 5% over 1 minute OR queue growth > 200% over baseline typically triggers phased.
[13:50] Liam: for our timeline: we want a pilot in EU+US in two months. what should we prioritize?
[13:55] Ava: prioritize policy templates, a dedicated standby pool in second region, and pre-warm set for top 50 prefixes. also security checklist for Private if you go that route.
[14:05] Nora: any gotchas for VPC peering or routing tables at the cloud provider?
[14:09] Marco: yes: make sure MTU and path MTU discovery is consistent; TCP windowing and health-probe routing can be affected by cloud NATs. for GCP/AWS interconnect there are specific BGP timers we advise. we'll include provider-specific notes.
[14:23] Amy: one final technical: how do you prevent split-brain on control plane? if two regions think they're primary?
[14:28] Priya: control plane uses quorum and region-leader election. read-only decisions can be local, but routing state changes use consensus. for Private deployments we can tie leader election to your control-plane gate.
[14:40] Marco: and we keep a single source-of-truth config in the control plane with versioned rollouts to avoid drift.
[14:46] Liam: ok good. I think that covers most tech areas. quick recap?
[14:49] Ava: recap: we'll share runbook, topology diagrams, degraded-mode and routing templates, and security docs. BlueOrbit to confirm regions and SLOs. Redwood to run cross-region bench with priya. schedule follow-up in two weeks.
[15:02] Liam: thanks all. any last words?
[15:05] Carlos: thanks. please mark anything that touches PII with a label in the runbook.
[15:09] Marco: will do.
[15:11] Ava: thanks everyone, we'll circulate materials. bye.
[15:15] (call ends)
file_notes: Transcription includes occasional mis-hearings (e.g., 'K-V cash' in places). Template YAML and routing policy referenced — to be attached separately by Marco in CRM notes.
